lesson_title: Map the Mountain: Differentiation Rules and Cubic Graphs
hook_text: Every cubic graph is a mountain footpath — and one derivative hands you the full trail report before you take a step.
clip_script: A cubic graph is a mountain footpath: climb, lookout, descent, valley floor, climb out forever. Calculus writes the trail report in advance. The derivative is the steepness underfoot at every stride. Where is the lookout? Where the steepness is zero — level ground. Take x cubed minus three x squared minus nine x plus twenty-seven. Differentiate with one rule — exponent falls forward, power steps down — to get three x squared minus six x minus nine. Set it to zero, factorise: level ground at x equals minus one and x equals three. Feed those back into the original function for altitudes: a lookout at height thirty-two, a valley floor at height zero. Where does the path drop? Wherever the derivative is negative — between minus one and three. And partway down, at x equals one, the path stops rolling over the crest and starts curving into the bowl — the inflection point, the steepest stride of the descent. One derivative, and the whole mountain is mapped: summit, valley, every rising and falling stretch. That is all a full cubic sketch question ever asks for — a trail report.
visual_style: A glowing cubic curve drawn as a ridge path in late-afternoon light, a walker dot tracing it, a steepness gauge sweeping to zero at the lookout and the valley floor, altitude labels popping, the descent shading red.
pacing: Steady climbing rhythm, a held beat at each level spot, a free-run finish up the last climb.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn every cubic sketch into a five-step trail report.
